title: Brands Are RL Environments
subtitle: Part one: we asked a new model to start a cloud kitchen from nothing. What came back says a lot about where slop comes from, and how to make brands that sell.

content.text: Ben Thompson ended his piece on Jensen Huang this week with a line that has been rattling around my head ever since: "It only takes an individual." His argument is that AI lets a very small number of people, or even just one person, do what used to take a company. He was talking about Nvidia. I keep thinking about a kitchen.

Specifically, I keep thinking about a small test we ran at ShopOS. The Sloosh team post-trained a new model, and we wanted to know how far it could go on its own. So we gave it one job: start a new cloud kitchen company. No brand book, no designer, no list of dishes. Just the job.

What came back was Pam's Kitchen, a homemade Indian dark kitchen in London. It came with a name, a daily ritual, a website, delivery app listings, five flyers, a one-page pamphlet, a thirty-one page coffee-table book, tote bags and t-shirts. More than forty pieces in all.

attrs.alt: The Pam's Kitchen delivery set: kraft box, steel tiffin, cotton tote.

content.text: The Pam's Kitchen delivery set: kraft box, steel tiffin, cotton tote.

Making one nice image is not interesting anymore; every tool can do that. What was interesting is that the forty pieces agreed with each other. They looked like one company. And the reason they did is the subject of this essay, because I think it explains two things at once: why so much of what AI makes for brands is slop, and what it would take to make brands that are good and also sell.
The short version is this: a brand is a reinforcement learning environment. Most brands just never designed theirs.
How Models Got Good at Code
To explain what I mean, it helps to start with why AI got so good at writing software in the first place.

The big jump in coding models over the last year did not come from reading more code. It came from reinforcement learning, or RL. The idea is old and simple. You put an agent in an environment. The agent sees the state of the world, takes an action, and gets a reward. Do that millions of times and the agent builds up a policy: a habit of taking the actions that tend to get rewarded.

The canonical example is AlphaGo, which beat Lee Sedol at Go in 2016 in large part by playing itself over and over and learning from wins and losses. The environment was a Go board. The reward was winning.

Code turned out to be a near-perfect environment for the same reason. When a model writes code, there is an obvious, cheap, automatic reward available: did the tests pass? The model tries something, the tests say yes or no, and the model learns. It can do that an enormous number of times without a human in the loop. Maths works the same way, because answers can be checked.
That is the important part. RL is only as good as its reward. Code and maths have rewards that are crisp, fast and hard to fake. That is why those domains moved first and fastest.

There is one more chapter of this history worth remembering, because it matters for brands. The reason ChatGPT felt so different from the models before it was not just scale; it was a technique called reinforcement learning from human feedback. OpenAI described it in its InstructGPT work in 2022: people compared pairs of model outputs and said which one was better, a separate "reward model" learned to predict those preferences, and then the main model was trained to score well against that reward model. In other words, when there was no test suite for "is this a helpful answer?", they built one out of human judgement.
Hold on to that idea. When a domain has no automatic reward, you can manufacture one from taste. That is the whole trick for brands, and almost nobody applies it there.
Now think about brands.
Why Brands Get Slop

A brand has no test suite. Nobody can run a script that says this flyer is good and that one is bad. The rewards that do exist are slow and noisy. A sale shows up days after the ad. Loyalty shows up over months. Weather, payday and luck all get mixed in.

So what happens when you point a model at a brand anyway? It optimises for whatever reward is closest to hand. Usually that is a click, a like, or a human glancing at the output and saying "looks fine." And this is where slop comes from.

RL researchers have a name for this failure: reward hacking. The agent finds a cheap way to get the reward without doing the thing you actually wanted. My favourite example is from OpenAI in 2016. They trained an agent on a boat racing game called CoastRunners, where points came from hitting targets along the course. The agent discovered it could score more by driving in a little circle, hitting the same targets over and over, catching fire, and never finishing the race. By the reward, it was winning. By any human standard, it had missed the point entirely.

Slop is that boat. Ask a model for a food brand and reward it on attention, and you get the circle: shouting headlines, fake discounts, glossy stock curry, "authentic flavours," fifty percent off forever. Each of those moves scores. Together they burn the brand down. People stop trusting it, and the sales follow a little later.
This is also just Goodhart's Law, usually paraphrased as "when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure." Clicks are a fine thing to measure. They are a terrible thing to aim at.
A Brand Is an Environment
Once you see the problem this way, the fix stops being "get a better model." The model is fine. The model is doing exactly what it was rewarded to do. The fix is to design the environment.
Look at what a brand actually is:
State:
where the brand is right now. Its name, voice, colours, customers, what it has said before.
Action:
every piece it makes. A name, a menu line, a photo, a flyer.
Reward:
what happens next. Did people order? Did they come back? Did they tell a friend?
Policy:
the brand's habits. "We always show the price." "We never say authentic."
That is an RL environment. Every brand already has one. The difference between great brands and forgettable ones is whether anyone designed it on purpose.

I find it useful to draw this as a 2x2. Across the bottom is how specific the work is: generic on the left, specific on the right. Up the side is whether it sells. Generic work that doesn't sell is slop. Generic work that does sell, for a while, is clickbait. Specific work that doesn't sell is an art project. Specific work that sells is a brand. The whole game is getting into the top right and staying there, and the only way I know to do that reliably is to shape the environment so that specific, honest work is what gets rewarded.
Brands Are a Long-Horizon Problem

I wrote a piece in September called Going outcome-first when you're AI-first, where I drew a 2x2 for a fund that wanted to understand how AI adoption was playing out with consumer brands. The axes were simple:

Across: how long the task runs. A short horizon task is done in one sitting. One image. One caption. One ad. A long horizon task keeps going. It has memory, follow-ups and a hundred small decisions stacked on top of each other.
Up: how hard it is to implement. Easy means one person with a good tool can do it. Hard means data, integrations, scale, approvals, and someone accountable when it breaks.

My point then was that the do-it-yourself AI tools are fantastic for the short, easy box: one listing image, one caption. Skip the agency there; skip us too. The trouble is that very few brands have their whole problem in that box.

A brand is the long-horizon task. It is a hundred small decisions stacked on top of each other: the name constrains the menu, the menu constrains the photos, the photos constrain the flyers, and the flyers have to sound like the website a customer saw three weeks ago. A short-horizon tool with no memory will make each decision fresh. Each one might look fine on its own. Together they drift, and drift is just slop that takes longer to notice.
That is the deeper reason the environment matters. An environment is memory. It is the thing that carries decision forty back to decision one.
What We Gave the Model

So how do you design a brand environment? For Pam's Kitchen, the answer was a stack of layers. This is how you break it down. You start with nothing. Then you lay on top of that the right skill files, models, workflows, brand sections, insights, guides, methodologies, and your own taste. Then you put it together.
None of those layers is the brand. Together, they make a world where good work is easy and slop is hard. Let me walk through each one as it played out in the kitchen.
Start with nothing

Nothing is never actually empty; it is whatever mess you already have. For Pam's Kitchen, the mess was three menus: a WhatsApp menu card with cartoon fonts and clip-art bowls, a 150-dish list in tiny text, and a weekly planner with tables and prices everywhere.

attrs.alt: The starting state: three menus, three looks.

content.text: The starting state: three menus, three looks.
Each of them sort of worked. Together they said "we don't know who we are yet," which is normal for any small food business. You cook first and brand later.

In RL terms this is the starting state, and the loudest thing about it was the 150-dish list. That list is a huge action space. A model looking at it could redesign 150 dishes, shoot 150 photos and write 150 descriptions, and that is exactly where slop breeds: everything gets a little attention and nothing gets enough.
So the first real move was a cut. One pot a day. Lock it by 9pm the night before. Cook only what's locked.

I love this move because it works on three levels at once. For customers, it removes decision fatigue; the only question is "do I want tomorrow's pot?" For the kitchen, it kills waste, because you cook what is locked and nothing more. And for the agent, it shrinks the action space from 150 things to one thing done well, repeated daily. Smaller action spaces learn faster and leave less room for slop.

It is also worth saying why a cloud kitchen was a good first environment at all. The episodes are short: one pot, one day, and by 9pm you know how many people locked. The cost of a bad episode is small; a pot nobody locks is a lesson, not a bankruptcy. And the customer is close. They message you on WhatsApp and tell you the dal was too salty. Compare that to a car company or a bank, where episodes take years and mistakes cost millions. You don't train a dog on a motorway. You train it in the living room, and a kitchen is the living room of brands.
Skill files

The first layer is skill files: short documents that teach the agent how to do one thing well. How to write a dish in one line. How to shoot food on steel instead of white plates. How to lay out an A5 flyer. Think of them as the house rules on the fridge, which every flatmate reads so nobody has to argue every week.

The most important skill file was a punish list. Never write "authentic." Never write "mouth-watering." No fake discounts. No stock photos. The price is the price. These sound small, but "authentic flavours" is the smell of slop; every curry house in the world says it. Banning it forces the agent to say something real.
Models

The second layer is models. Different models are good at different jobs: one writes well, one makes great food photography, one is good at layout. In RL terms these are the actors. Just as important is the critic, a model whose only job is to look at every output and ask whether it would embarrass us. People skip the critic. That is a mistake, because the critic is the cheapest taste you can buy.
Workflows
The third layer is the workflow, the order of operations. For Pam's Kitchen it went ritual, name, menu, site, print, book, merch.

Ritual before name sounds backwards, but the name has to carry the ritual. "Pam's Kitchen" sounds like a person, a real home cook, and that fits a homemade pot that drops daily. A clever tech name would have fought it. In RL this is called a curriculum: you teach easy things first and build up. A dog learns sit before it learns fetch.
The name itself went through its own episode. The model sketched dozens of lettering directions, traced the strongest one, and inked it.
Lettering studies for the name.
The chosen direction, traced.

attrs.alt: Inked by hand, half pencil, half walnut ink.

content.text: Inked by hand, half pencil, half walnut ink.
It also explored whole logo systems before landing: a Devanagari-inspired wordmark, a sweet-shop seal, an arched badge for dark backgrounds, and the stacked script that won.

attrs.alt: Four logo directions. The stacked script on the right won.

content.text: Four logo directions. The stacked script on the right won.
Brand sections

The fourth layer is the brand book, split into sections: voice, colour, type, photography, price, story. Each section is a constraint, and constraints are the friend of creativity, not its enemy. A blank page is terrifying; a page with three rules is a game.
Pam's Kitchen got bottle green and ghee cream, a warm serif, steel tiffins and kraft boxes, and real-looking food that is never glossy.
The brand board.

attrs.alt: Bottle green, walnut, ghee cream, brass.

content.text: Bottle green, walnut, ghee cream, brass.

attrs.alt: A display face with Kannada DNA.

content.text: A display face with Kannada DNA.
Every later piece had to pass these rules. That is how forty pieces end up looking like one company.

It is worth dwelling on why these particular rules worked. Bottle green and ghee cream are colours of a home kitchen, not a restaurant chain; nobody's mother cooks under neon orange. Steel and brass are what the food is actually served in back home, so the props carry a truth that no styling could fake. And the rule that food must look real, never glossy, does something subtle: it lowers the ceiling on how impressive any single photo can be, in exchange for raising the floor on how trustworthy all of them are. That is a trade a slop-optimising agent would never make on its own, because glossy photos win the glance. A brand environment has to make it for the agent, in advance, so the agent never gets the chance to chase the glance.
Insights

The fifth layer is insights: things you know about real people. They don't come from the model. They come from life. Indian students in London miss home food. Their mums worry they aren't eating properly. Londoners love a crispy galette. Nobody wants to pick from 150 dishes on a Tuesday.

Each insight is a little map that tells the agent where the reward probably is. Watch what happens when one meets an action: on the delivery apps, the masala dosa listing says "If you like a crispy galette." It translates an Indian dish into a word Londoners already love. No model invents that line from nothing; it comes from knowing who is ordering.

attrs.alt: On the apps: "If you like a crispy galette."

content.text: On the apps: "If you like a crispy galette."
Guides

The sixth layer is guides, which are worked examples, good and bad. You can't describe taste in a rule; you can only point at it. For the menu, the guide was a set of one-line dish stories. Paneer butter masala, "the one Delhi made famous." Idli, "the batter that rises overnight." Medu vada, "the savoury doughnut." Once the model saw ten of these, it could write a hundred.

attrs.alt: The menu, by region, a story for every dish.

content.text: The menu, by region, a story for every dish.

Guides also set the dial between exploration and exploitation. Some examples were safe: a clean photo, a price, a QR code. Some were wild on purpose: recipes smuggled out of India in a tin of ghee. The wild ones told the model it was allowed to play. The safe ones told it where home was.
The food photography is where the guides show up most. Every dish sits on the same green plaster or walnut table, in steel or brass, in soft window light.
Appam and vegetable stew.
Kerala fish moilee.
Medu vada, delivered.
A work-from-home lunch, opened up.

On a delivery app you sit in a list of fifty kitchens, and most of the thumbnails look random. Pam's looks like one brand in every tile. The model didn't choose that consistency; the guides and brand sections forced it.
Methodologies
The seventh layer is the methodology: how the work gets scored. This is where the RL framing gets real, because this is the reward.

The honest problem with brands, again, is that the real reward is slow. RL people call this a sparse reward: the treat comes so rarely that the agent can't tell which action earned it. The answer is to add dense rewards, small signals that show up fast and point toward the big one.

For a cloud kitchen the dense signals are easy to list. Did people lock tomorrow's pot by 9pm? How many locks came from each WhatsApp message? Did they come back next week? Did anyone screenshot the flyer? On top of those sits a critic rubric with five questions: Could any other kitchen have said this? Is there a real detail in it? Does it sound like a person? Does it point back at the ritual? Would we be embarrassed to hand it to a neighbour?

The sparse reward stays the boss: sales, repeat sales, margin. The dense rewards are breadcrumbs. The trick is never letting a breadcrumb become the goal, because that is the boat going in circles again.
Taste

The eighth layer is your own taste. This is the layer everyone hopes to skip. They hope the model has taste built in, and in a sense it does: it has the average taste of the internet. Which is exactly the problem. The average of the internet is slop. Your taste is the part that isn't average.
In RL terms, taste is the reward model. It is the thing that says "more of this" and "never again." The loop looks like this:

The model makes twenty versions. The critic kills most of them. A human looks at the last few and picks one, or kills them all. Every kill becomes a line in a guide, and the next round starts smarter. Generation is cheap now; judgement is the scarce thing.
The flyers are the clearest example. One of them reads: "Your mum called. She says you're not eating properly. We're handling it. £4.99." And at the bottom: "p.s. call her back."
Five flyers. Stories, not ads.

That flyer is an insight wearing a joke. The insight gave the story, the guide gave the voice, the brand sections gave the green and the serif, the punish list kept out the discount badge, and taste kept the p.s.

It is worth tracing that episode more slowly, because it shows how the layers interact. It starts with a blank A5. The skill file says how an A5 flyer works: one headline, a short story, one action, a p.s. The model drafts twenty stories, and most of them are fine, which is the problem; fine is the enemy. The insight layer pushes one angle forward: students miss home, mums worry. The critic then runs its first question, "could any other kitchen have said this?", and most of the twenty die right there. "Delicious home food, delivered!" is dead. "Taste of home, at your door!" is dead. A few survive, a human reads them out loud, and one makes the room laugh. Then the human adds the last line. The model did not write "p.s. call her back"; the taste layer did. And now the guide has one more example, so next time the model knows a p.s. can land.
That is one episode: twenty actions, one reward, one lesson saved. Forty of those is a brand.
Putting It Together
The last step is putting it together, and this is where the forty pieces show up. Everything hangs off one line: one pot a day, lock it tonight.

The website opens with the price in the headline. Most food brands hide the price; Pam's puts it front and centre, because cheap-but-homemade is the pitch and hiding it would be a small lie. Small lies are where slop starts.

attrs.alt: The hero: "A home-cooked pot drops every day. It's £4.99."

content.text: The hero: "A home-cooked pot drops every day. It's £4.99."

The weekly rhythm is spelled out as pot, lock, drop: the idli pot on Monday, the paneer pot on Tuesday, a party pot on Saturday. And on Friday, the pot rests. That one line makes the whole thing feel like a real person runs it, a tired, happy person who takes Fridays off. You cannot prompt for "human touches." You get them from an environment that rewards specifics.

attrs.alt: Pot, lock, drop. Friday, the pot rests.

content.text: Pot, lock, drop. Friday, the pot rests.
Then it goes physical. A menu card for the bag. A kraft box with a green band. A tote at the door. A delivery landing on a London kitchen counter.
Today's pot, on cotton paper.
Delivered.
At the door.

attrs.alt: The customer the brand is really for.

content.text: The customer the brand is really for.
Then the one-page pamphlet, built so a neighbour gets the whole idea in ten seconds, because local food still lives on paper: letterboxes, office kitchens, temple and gurdwara notice boards.

attrs.alt: One A4 page. Hand it to anyone.

content.text: One A4 page. Hand it to anyone.

Then the coffee-table book, "Pam's Kitchens of India," thirteen dishes and thirteen places, including chicken tikka masala, credited to "Glasgow, via Punjab." That is the voice: playful, true and a little nerdy. A thirty-one page book is also the hardest test of the environment, because long episodes are where drift happens. The colours held. The voice held.
Pam's Kitchens of India.
The bound menu.
And finally the tees, which sound silly for a kitchen and are also the cheapest billboard in London.
Bottle green, tonal print.
The full set.
The Model as a New Hire
If the RL language feels abstract, there is a more human way to think about all of this: onboarding.

Think about how you would bring a great new designer into a studio. You would not hand them one sentence and say "make our brand good." You would sit them down and show them the best work you have ever done. You would show them the worst work, and explain why it was bad. You would tell them stories about customers. You would tell them the words you never use. You would check their first ten pieces closely, the next fifty less closely, and by month three they would just get it. They would have absorbed the environment.

That is exactly what the layers do for a model. Skill files are the onboarding doc. Guides are the portfolio review. Insights are the customer stories. The punish list is the banned words. The critic is the senior designer. You are the creative director.

The difference is speed and stamina. A new hire takes three months to absorb the environment and starts to forget bits of it by Friday afternoon. The model takes an afternoon and never forgets. It writes the hundredth dish story as carefully as the first, and it never gets bored of the brand book. What it cannot do is decide what the environment should be. That part is still yours.
Closing the Loop

All of this would be theory without the street, so it is worth being concrete about what the loop looks like once a brand like this is live. If I were running the first month of Pam's Kitchen, I would watch a deliberately small dashboard: locks per night, locks per WhatsApp message sent, the share of people who lock again in week two, pamphlet QR scans by street, uptake of the Saturday party pot, and the screenshots and forwards people tell you about.

None of those is a sale on its own. Each is a breadcrumb toward one, and each can feed back into the critic. If the "your mum called" flyer drives locks, the guide gets more lines like it. If the "confidential" flyer gets ignored, somebody should find out why before the model makes five more like it. That is the loop closing: the street trains the critic, the critic trains the drafts, and the drafts go back out to the street.

The important discipline is to keep the sparse reward in charge. It would be easy to optimise the kitchen for screenshots and end up with a very funny brand that nobody orders from. The breadcrumbs are there to make the slow reward legible, not to replace it.
Isn't This Just a Brand Book?
The obvious objection to all of this is that I have described a brand book with extra steps. And yes, sort of. But the difference matters.

A brand book is a frozen environment. Someone wrote it once, usually at the end of an expensive project. Nobody updates it. It sits in a shared drive, and new designers skim it on their first day. Its rules are enforced only when a tired senior person happens to notice a violation.

The environment I am describing is alive. It has a critic that reads every rule on every output, every time. It has rewards that point at money, not just at consistency. It has a punish list that grows every time something cheap sneaks through. And it learns: every kill becomes a new guide line, every signal from the street tunes the critic.
A brand book tells you the rules. An environment enforces them, and writes new ones while it works.

There is a second difference, which is economic. A business like Pam's Kitchen could never have afforded a full brand before. A book, a pamphlet, five flyers, a food shoot and app listings used to be a meaningful agency engagement, well out of reach for a one-person kitchen. The model inside an environment collapses that cost. Small businesses get a real brand, with a voice and a reason to exist, instead of a template from a logo maker. That, more than any single image, is the part that excites me.
Where the Value Goes
Let me zoom out, because I think this test says something bigger than "AI can make a nice brand."

Ben Thompson has written for years about integration and modularity, borrowing from Clayton Christensen: profits flow away from the parts of a value chain that become modular and interchangeable, and toward the parts that stay integrated and differentiated. In AI, the question has been whether the models themselves get commoditised.

For creative work, I think the answer is that models are increasingly the modular part. You can swap one image model for another; we do, constantly. What is not modular is the environment: the skill files, the guides, the punish list, the critic's rubric, the insights about real customers, and the taste that decides what gets killed. That is the integrated piece. That is where a brand's quality actually lives.

That is also, not coincidentally, what a great creative studio is. A great studio is an environment. Years of taste, a sharp eye for what kills a piece, a pile of guides nobody ever wrote down, and a gut for what sells. Most of it lives in a few people's heads. When they are tired, it slips. When they leave, it walks out the door.

This is why we are building ShopOS the way we are: an AI lab that rolls up creative studios, so that the internet isn't full of slop. The point is not to replace studios. The point is to write their environments down, put models inside them, and let a studio's taste run at the speed of software while the humans spend their time on the hard calls.
What the Framing Bought Us
So what did thinking about brands as RL environments actually buy us?
First, a precise way to talk about slop. Slop is reward hacking: an agent chasing a cheap signal. Once you see it that way you stop blaming the model and start fixing the environment.
Second, a way to scale taste. Taste used to live in one person's mood on a Tuesday. Now it lives in files the model reads every single time.
Third, a way to connect craft to sales. The dense rewards are craft signals; the sparse reward is money. A good environment makes every craft signal point at a sale, and if one doesn't, you cut it.

Fourth, and most important, compounding. A normal brand project ends when the agency hands over the files. An environment keeps learning: every kill adds a guide line, every street signal tunes the critic, and the hundredth flyer is better than the first, not because anyone worked harder but because the world got wiser.

There are honest limits. Brands are not Go. A kitchen gets one episode a day, not millions, so most of the learning happens in simulation (drafts, mockups, critic scores) and a few precious real episodes on the street. When the street disagrees with the critic, the street wins and the critic gets updated. Insights still come from living, not from the model. And somebody still has to say no.
It Only Takes an Environment

I'll come back to where I started. "It only takes an individual" is true, but I think it is incomplete. An individual with a model and no environment makes slop, very quickly. An individual with a model inside a well-designed environment makes a brand.
Pam's Kitchen is our first test: one pot a day, forty pieces, one voice.

If you want to try this on your own brand, start smaller than you think. Pick the one cut that removes most choices. Write five banned words and five real specifics about your customer. Collect ten examples you love and five you hate. Then let a model explore inside that box, kill most of what comes back, and write down why. Do it again tomorrow. Within a week you will notice the drafts getting less sloppy, not because the model changed, but because the world around it did.
Part two
is a harder world: a physical product, a car perfume made from nothing, where the rewards are slower and the gap between a render and your hand is much wider.
p.s. If you run a small food business and want to try this on yours, reply. I'd love to see your three messy menus.
